Out of the Box with Original Thinking

Original thinking is the ability to think outside the box, to look at a problem, and to figure out a new, creative solution for it. Many people choose to safely follow the path others have already paved, but it is difficult to achieve something exceptional in this way. More often those who think differently achieve lasting success because to address the challenges of tomorrow, it's essential to adopt a fresh approach distinct from yesterday. So, how can individuals cultivate original thinking that leads to outstanding achievements?

Generate a Lot of Ideas

If you want to have good ideas, you must have numerous ideas. Traditionally, people follow the saying that they prefer "quality over quantity." However, in the case of ideas, quantity and quality are equally important. Highly creative individuals do not actually produce better ideas than average ones. Instead, they produce more ideas. Their increased idea output means that they are more likely to hit on something brilliant.

An excellent example is Pablo Picasso. Picasso is famous for a handful of artworks. However, few people realize that Picasso's portfolio includes 2,800 ceramics, 1,800 paintings, 1,200 sculptures, and more than 12,000 drawings. Again, only a fraction of them became famous. Likewise, Mozart composed over 600 pieces before his death at age 35, only a handful of which are recognized as particularly creative. Einstein also had more than 248 publications, but many of them didn't have much impact. The lesson here is to produce a large volume of work. This way, you have more of a chance that one or two will be outstanding. Just pour out whatever comes to mind and separate the gems from the rocks.

Don't Rush

We are frequently told that procrastination is our worst enemy. Almost every self-help book describes successful people as being those who can overcome procrastination. However, several moments of genius have stemmed from procrastination. Great originals know how to utilize procrastination as a strategy in their idea production. Procrastination encourages gradual progress rather than rapid progress, which leaves your brain open to a wider range of ideas. While procrastination may be the enemy of productivity, it can be a resource for creativity.

Few people know that Leonardo da Vinci was a chronic procrastinator. It took him 16 years to complete the Mona Lisa. Some of the things that took his attention away from work, like learning optics, transformed the way he modeled light and made him into a much better painter.

What about Martin Luther King, Jr.? The original script of his speech, believe it or not, didn't contain the words "I have a dream." The night before the biggest speech of his life, he was up past 3 a.m. rewriting his script. He was sitting in the audience waiting for his turn to go onto the stage and still writing notes on his script. After he got on stage, 11 minutes in, he heard Mahalia Jackson, his favorite singer, cry out: "Tell them about the dream, Martin." Encouraged by a shout from the audience, he drew upon some of his past talks, and the result became the landmark speech "I have a dream." By delaying the task of finalizing the speech until the very last minute, he left himself open to the widest range of possible ideas. The text wasn't set in stone, and he had the freedom to improvise.

Fight the Status Quo

The hallmark of originality is rejecting the default and finding out if a better option exists. Your ability to do things differently, to question and refine the way things work is what makes you creative and different. Your Internet browser is a pain? Change it! You don't like the system? Say so! You have a new idea? Try it! You see a better way of doing things? Test it! Most people won't take any risk. They'll just stick with what they know, thinking it'll be good enough. But if you think that you can change things, then your originality and your creativity could make a big difference in the end.

The founders of an online eyewear company, for instance, couldn't understand why it was so hard to find an affordable pair of glasses. They thought the problem was interesting, so they conducted some research. They found that just one company dominated 80% of the market. As a result, they created a company that no one expected to thrive. Instead of depending on only physical stores where customers could try the eyeglasses on directly, they created a business where you could simply order inexpensive, high-quality eyewear online. Using this business model, they were able to offer glasses that normally cost $500 for only $95. In addition, every time a customer purchased glasses from them, they'd make a donation to charities. All of this was possible because they sold on the Internet.

The online eyewear company has, without a doubt, been successful. It was voted as the most innovative business by a world-leading business magazine. The company grew to be worth more than a billion dollars. Anyone could have noticed the problem with expensive glasses in stores, but it took courageous pioneers to find the answers. Rules and systems are made by people. This means they can be changed by people as well. It's a good idea to challenge the defaults.

We often believe that original insight is primarily a matter of nature: you are either born with it, or you aren't. But from a different perspective, it can be nurtured. The above stories, however, show that original thinking can be improved through our effort. It turns out that we are all original thinkers in process.
title: Out of the Box with Original Thinking
